1

Introduction
Chemi-ions:
Ions naturally produced within the combustion reaction of hydrocarbon
ﬂames.
How do external electric ﬁeld eﬀects produce observed ﬂame reactions?
Explanations:
1. Electronic thermal eﬀect
joule heating increasing ﬂame temperatures.
2. Electronic chemical eﬀect
highly energized electrons enhancing reaction rates.
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
mechanical drag on bulk gas by migrating ions.
2

Introduction
1. Electronic thermal eﬀect
Jaggers and Engel (1971)
▶combustion power - ∼104W
▶electrical power - ∼1W
2. Electronic chemical eﬀect
▶not well deﬁned
▶Fialkov (1997)
comprehensive survey of literature concluded,
“a high-frequency electric ﬁeld aﬀects the propagating ﬂame velocity, but
shows little or no eﬀect on the burning velocity of the ﬂame on the burner.”
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
Majority of electric ﬁeld combustion community agree that ion wind
theory could almost completely account for the observed eﬀects.
3

Purpose
Importance of micro-gravity:
▶Ion winds compete with buoyancy and initial jet velocity.
▶International Space Station µg experiments are scheduled to begin
in 2017.
▶This will isolate only ion winds.
Goals for this study:
▶Demonstrate the importance of ion current measurements.
▶Characterize current-voltage (I-V) curves for burner conﬁgurations
that will be used in ISS experiments.
▶Determine the source of ion currents above saturation levels.
▶1g experiments provide the tools needed to analyze µg experiments.

Discussion
What is the source of the super-saturation ion currents?
Possible sources:
1. Electrical breakdown
▶global breakdown - unlikely
(since ﬁeld strengths ≪25kV/cm)
▶local breakdown - likely
(corona discharge, thermal ionization)
2. Electron Avalanche
▶more likely to occur with negative ﬁeld strengths.
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
▶enhancement to gas ﬂow dynamics enhancing local mixing leading to
enhanced chemi-ionization reaction rates.
10

Conclusions
1. local breakdown does occur.
2. local breakdown can be active participant.
3. local breakdown is not the initial source of enhanced ion current
saturation.

Figure: Weinberg and Carleton (2009).
Conclusions
1. 0-70% air admixture
no discernible changes in saturation ion currents
2. 85-94.7% air admixture
large changes in saturation ion currents

Conclusion
1. Secondary ionization mechanisms can occur even with ﬁeld
strengths below electrical breakdown.
▶examples: local breakdown.
▶are not the main source of increasing ion currents above saturation.
2. Ion winds do inﬂuence ﬂame geometry.
▶enhances local mixing.
▶partially-premixed regions leads to high ion current.
3. Importance and usefulness of ion current measurements were
demonstrated.
